question: A nonexempt employee of an enterprise covered by the FLSA worked 46 compensable hours in one workweek. What minimum overtime rate must apply to the six hours above 40?

citations.quoted_text: For a workweek longer than forty hours ... compensation for his employment in excess of the hours above specified at a rate not less than one and one-half times the regular rate at which he is employed.
citations.support_explanation: This provision supplies both the 40-hour threshold and the minimum overtime rate applicable to the six hours beyond it.

legal_materials.provision_text: Except as otherwise provided in this section, no employer shall employ any of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, or is employed in an enterprise engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, for a workweek longer than forty hours unless such employee receives compensation for his employment in excess of the hours above specified at a rate not less than one and one-half times the regular rate at which he is employed.

analysis_summary: The supplied provision sets a 40-hour workweek threshold and requires compensation at not less than 1.5 times the regular rate for hours worked beyond that threshold. The question stipulates that the employee is nonexempt and covered, and identifies the six excess hours.

question: On June 1, 2024, may an employer pay $7.00 per hour to an employee covered by the federal minimum-wage provision, if the question is limited to the federal statutory floor?

citations.support_explanation: The quoted rate establishes the federal minimum specified in the supplied provision and therefore does not permit payment at $7.00 per hour under that floor.

legal_materials.version_or_effective_period: The $7.25 rate took effect on July 24, 2009; text in force on 2024-06-01
legal_materials.provision_text: Every employer shall pay to each of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, or is employed in an enterprise engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, wages at the following rates: ... $7.25 an hour, beginning on July 24, 2009.

analysis_summary: The question limits the issue to the federal statutory floor and stipulates that the employee is covered by the provision. The quoted text specifies a rate of $7.25 per hour, which is higher than the proposed $7.00 rate.
